docs.body:
Copy a byte range the caller has validated into linear memory.

 The caller must ensure that `dest` has room for `len` bytes in a live
 allocation. The range is validated only against a length the caller
 was given, which may exceed the input, so the copy must stay safe for
 any source range: an implementation may skip the check only where
 reading past the end is itself safe, as calldata reads zeros there.
 Arbitrary byte lengths are supported.

 `ByteInput`, which every `ByteSource` is.

 only `Copy` inputs can be stored, as in `Cursor` and `BytesView`.

pub fn decode_frame_from<A: Abi, T, I>(_ input: I, _ pos: u256, _ input_len: u256) -> T
    where T: Decode<A> + AbiSize,

items.signature:
use super::intrinsic
use super::marker::Copy
use super::num::IntDowncast
use super::ops::{Eq, Index}

/// Number of words needed for a fixed-width byte sequence, without rounding overflow.
const fn word_len(_ n: usize) -> usize {
    n / 32 + if n % 32 == 0 { 0 } else { 1 }
}

/// An owned, fixed-width byte sequence stored in big-endian numeric words.
/// Byte zero is the most significant byte of word zero. Unused tail bytes are zero.
/// Ordinary byte arrays cross this boundary explicitly through `from_array`/`to_array`.
pub struct PackedBytes<const N: usize> { words: [u256; word_len(N)] }

impl<const N: usize> Copy for PackedBytes<N> {}

impl<const N: usize> PackedBytes<N> {
    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn zero() -> Self {
        Self { words: [0; word_len(N)] }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn len(self) -> usize {
        N
    }

    /// Returns a numeric word. The last word is padded on the right with zeros.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn word(self, _ index: usize) -> u256 {
        self.words[index]
    }
    pub const fn from_array(_ bytes: [u8; N]) -> Self {
        var out = ByteWriter<N>::new()
        out.push_array(bytes)
        out.finish()
    }
    pub const fn to_array(self) -> [u8; N] {
        var out: [u8; N] = [0; N]
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < N {
            out[i] = self[i]
            i += 1
        }
        out
    }
}

impl<const N: usize> Index<usize> for PackedBytes<N> {
    type Output = u8

    #[inline(always)]
    const fn index(self, _ index: usize) -> ref u8 {
        assert!(index < N)
        let shift: u256 = ((31 - index % 32) * 8) as u256
        let byte: u8 = (self.words[index / 32] >> shift).downcast_truncate()
        ref byte
    }
}

impl<const N: usize> Eq for PackedBytes<N> {
    const fn eq(self, _ other: Self) -> bool {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < word_len(N) {
            if self.words[i] != other.words[i] {
                return false
            }
            i += 1
        }
        true
    }

    const fn ne(self, _ other: Self) -> bool {
        !self.eq(other)
    }
}

/// Appends into one packed destination. Every write checks the remaining capacity.
/// The cursor only grows; callers cannot obtain mutable references to stored bytes.
pub struct ByteWriter<const M: usize> { bytes: PackedBytes<M>, len: usize }

impl<const M: usize> ByteWriter<M> {
    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn new() -> Self {
        Self { bytes: PackedBytes<M>::zero(), len: 0 }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn finish(own self) -> PackedBytes<M> {
        assert!(self.len == M)
        self.bytes
    }

    /// Appends exactly the byte count promised by this component.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn append<T: AsBytes>(mut self, _ value: T) {
        let start = self.len
        value.append_to(mut self)
        assert!(self.len - start == T::N)
    }

    /// Appends the low `width` bytes in big-endian order, ignoring higher bits.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_word(mut self, _ value: u256, width: usize) {
        assert!(width <= 32)
        if width != 0 {
            self.push_aligned(value << (((32 - width) * 8) as u256), width)
        }
    }

    /// Appends the high `width` bytes of `value`, a nonzero count whose
    /// lower bytes are zero.
    #[inline(always)]
    const fn push_aligned(mut self, _ value: u256, width: usize) {
        assert!(width <= M - self.len)
        let r = self.len % 32
        self.bytes.words[self.len / 32] |= value >> ((r * 8) as u256)
        if r + width > 32 {
            self.bytes.words[self.len / 32 + 1] |= value << (((32 - r) * 8) as u256)
        }
        self.len += width
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_byte(mut self, _ value: u8) {
        self.push_word(value as u256, width: 1)
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_bytes<const K: usize>(mut self, _ value: PackedBytes<K>) {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < K / 32 {
            self.push_aligned(value.word(i), width: 32)
            i += 1
        }
        if K % 32 != 0 {
            self.push_aligned(value.word(i), width: K % 32)
        }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_array<const K: usize>(mut self, _ value: [u8; K]) {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < K / 32 {
            var word: u256 = 0
            var byte: usize = 0
            while byte < 32 {
                word = (word << 8) | (value[i * 32 + byte] as u256)
                byte += 1
            }
            self.push_aligned(word, width: 32)
            i += 1
        }
        var word: u256 = 0
        var byte: usize = 0
        while byte < K % 32 {
            word = (word << 8) | (value[K / 32 * 32 + byte] as u256)
            byte += 1
        }
        self.push_word(word, width: K % 32)
    }
}

/// Fixed-width, big-endian serialization shared by CTFE and runtime.
/// Implementations append exactly N bytes; tuples share one checked destination.
pub trait AsBytes {
    const N: usize
    /// Append exactly N bytes without replacing or rewinding the writer.
    const fn append_to<const M: usize>(self, _ out: mut ByteWriter<M>)

    #[inline(always)]
    const fn as_bytes(self) -> PackedBytes<Self::N> {
        var out = ByteWriter<Self::N>::new()
        out.append(self)
        out.finish()
    }
}

impl<const LEN: usize> AsBytes for [u8; LEN] {
    const N: usize = LEN
    #[inline(always)]
    const fn append_to<const M: usize>(self, _ out: mut ByteWriter<M>) {
        out.push_array(self)
    }
}

impl<const LEN: usize> AsBytes for PackedBytes<LEN> {

use super::intrinsic
use super::marker::Copy
use super::num::IntDowncast
use super::ops::{Eq, Index}

/// Number of words needed for a fixed-width byte sequence, without rounding overflow.
const fn word_len(_ n: usize) -> usize {
    n / 32 + if n % 32 == 0 { 0 } else { 1 }
}

/// An owned, fixed-width byte sequence stored in big-endian numeric words.
/// Byte zero is the most significant byte of word zero. Unused tail bytes are zero.
/// Ordinary byte arrays cross this boundary explicitly through `from_array`/`to_array`.
pub struct PackedBytes<const N: usize> { words: [u256; word_len(N)] }

impl<const N: usize> Copy for PackedBytes<N> {}

impl<const N: usize> PackedBytes<N> {
    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn zero() -> Self {
        Self { words: [0; word_len(N)] }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn len(self) -> usize {
        N
    }

    /// Returns a numeric word. The last word is padded on the right with zeros.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn word(self, _ index: usize) -> u256 {
        self.words[index]
    }
    pub const fn from_array(_ bytes: [u8; N]) -> Self {
        var out = ByteWriter<N>::new()
        out.push_array(bytes)
        out.finish()
    }
    pub const fn to_array(self) -> [u8; N] {
        var out: [u8; N] = [0; N]
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < N {
            out[i] = self[i]
            i += 1
        }
        out
    }
}

impl<const N: usize> Index<usize> for PackedBytes<N> {
    type Output = u8

    #[inline(always)]
    const fn index(self, _ index: usize) -> ref u8 {
        assert!(index < N)
        let shift: u256 = ((31 - index % 32) * 8) as u256
        let byte: u8 = (self.words[index / 32] >> shift).downcast_truncate()
        ref byte
    }
}

impl<const N: usize> Eq for PackedBytes<N> {
    const fn eq(self, _ other: Self) -> bool {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < word_len(N) {
            if self.words[i] != other.words[i] {
                return false
            }
            i += 1
        }
        true
    }

    const fn ne(self, _ other: Self) -> bool {
        !self.eq(other)
    }
}

/// Appends into one packed destination. Every write checks the remaining capacity.
/// The cursor only grows; callers cannot obtain mutable references to stored bytes.
pub struct ByteWriter<const M: usize> { bytes: PackedBytes<M>, len: usize }

impl<const M: usize> ByteWriter<M> {
    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn new() -> Self {
        Self { bytes: PackedBytes<M>::zero(), len: 0 }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub(ingot) const fn finish(own self) -> PackedBytes<M> {
        assert!(self.len == M)
        self.bytes
    }

    /// Appends exactly the byte count promised by this component.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn append<T: AsBytes>(mut self, _ value: T) {
        let start = self.len
        value.append_to(mut self)
        assert!(self.len - start == T::N)
    }

    /// Appends the low `width` bytes in big-endian order, ignoring higher bits.
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_word(mut self, _ value: u256, width: usize) {
        assert!(width <= 32)
        if width != 0 {
            self.push_aligned(value << (((32 - width) * 8) as u256), width)
        }
    }

    /// Appends the high `width` bytes of `value`, a nonzero count whose
    /// lower bytes are zero.
    #[inline(always)]
    const fn push_aligned(mut self, _ value: u256, width: usize) {
        assert!(width <= M - self.len)
        let r = self.len % 32
        self.bytes.words[self.len / 32] |= value >> ((r * 8) as u256)
        if r + width > 32 {
            self.bytes.words[self.len / 32 + 1] |= value << (((32 - r) * 8) as u256)
        }
        self.len += width
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_byte(mut self, _ value: u8) {
        self.push_word(value as u256, width: 1)
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_bytes<const K: usize>(mut self, _ value: PackedBytes<K>) {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < K / 32 {
            self.push_aligned(value.word(i), width: 32)
            i += 1
        }
        if K % 32 != 0 {
            self.push_aligned(value.word(i), width: K % 32)
        }
    }

    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn push_array<const K: usize>(mut self, _ value: [u8; K]) {
        var i: usize = 0
        while i < K / 32 {
            var word: u256 = 0
            var byte: usize = 0
            while byte < 32 {
                word = (word << 8) | (value[i * 32 + byte] as u256)
                byte += 1
            }
            self.push_aligned(word, width: 32)
            i += 1
        }
        var word: u256 = 0
        var byte: usize = 0
        while byte < K % 32 {
            word = (word << 8) | (value[K / 32 * 32 + byte] as u256)
            byte += 1
        }
        self.push_word(word, width: K % 32)
    }
}

/// Fixed-width, big-endian serialization shared by CTFE and runtime.
/// Implementations append exactly N bytes; tuples share one checked destination.
pub trait AsBytes {
    const N: usize
    /// Append exactly N bytes without replacing or rewinding the writer.
    const fn append_to<const M: usize>(self, _ out: mut ByteWriter<M>)

    #[inline(always)]
    const fn as_bytes(self) -> PackedBytes<Self::N> {
        var out = ByteWriter<Self::N>::new()
        out.append(self)
        out.finish()
    }
}

    const N: usize = LEN
    #[inline(always)]

items.name: functional

docs.body:
Core functional abstractions built around higher-kinded types.

 This module defines:
 - `Fn<shape A>` and `FnMut<shape A>`: callable values.
 - `Functor`: type constructors that can be mapped over.
 - `Applicative`: type constructors that support `pure` and `<*>`.
 - `Monad`: type constructors that support `bind`/`flat_map`.

 These traits are designed for types of kind `* -> *`, such as `Option`
 or partially applied types like `Result<E>`.
 A callable value taking the parameters its shape `A` lists:
 `Fn(own T, U) -> R` is `Fn<(own T, U), Out = R>`, and `-> _` leaves
 `Out` open. A call `f(x)` of a callable value runs its `Fn` `call`, or
 its `FnMut` `call_mut`. Closures and function items implement both traits
 at the shape of their own parameters. `uses E` is the row of effects a
 call runs: those a closure's body uses, or a function's own.

items.name: hint

docs.body:
Returns `value` unchanged while hiding it from the optimizer.

 The compiler must assume the call can observe `value`, change it and
 have other effects. The computation that produces `value` is kept even
 when the result is unused, and the call stays ordered with respect to
 other effects, such as reading the remaining gas. Pass a benchmark's
 inputs through `black_box` after the first gas read and its result
 before the second one:

 ```fe
 let gas_before = evm.gas()
 black_box(most_significant_bit(black_box(x)))
 let used = gas_before - evm.gas()
 ```

 `T` must be an integer-valued scalar type, such as an integer or `bool`.
 Pointers and aggregates are not supported.
 Only EVM targets support `black_box`.

docs.body:
A traversal of a base collection, `Base`, that a loop holds and passes to
 each call. A driver stores its state and parameters, never the base, so
 it is an ordinary value: built, stored and returned, and run over a base
 by `xs.by(d)`.

 Each position yields a `Step`: the element accesses it projects, with
 what the driver adds beside them, such as an index. A loop's pattern
 destructures it as a `let` does, and a closure the driver calls takes it
 whole.

 Nothing promises one call per element: `filter` projects each element to
 test it and again to yield it, and `take(0)` still starts its inner
 traversal.

docs.body:
A `Copy` type a view parameter takes by copy, a *snapshot*: a scalar or a
 handle, such as `Address` or a memory buffer's handle, whose copy is all a
 callee can observe. Primitives and raw pointers are snapshots without it.
 Every other value, `Copy` or not, is viewed in place: the call reads the
 caller's place for its duration, and a projection's result over it is the
 caller's place.

docs.body:
A type pinned to a state space: a value of it, and every place in it,
 lies in `Space` wherever it is held, so it and any type holding it are
 state-only. `Space` is `Storage` or `Transient`, or another pinned
 type's, `P::Space`. A state space starts zeroed: a slot no one wrote
 reads as zero, so state holds only types whose all-zero representation
 is a value, those without `unsafe` fields.
 A storage collection is pinned (`StateIndex`), and so is a cell such as
 `TSlot`.

docs.body:
A type whose all-zero representation is a value, so a stored value is
 cleared by zeroing its slots and lanes: scalars, raw pointers and
 aggregates of clearable types without `unsafe` fields. A type with
 `unsafe` fields is not, since they carry an invariant zero need not
 satisfy; nor is a storage collection, since its entries lie outside its
 own slots, so nothing holding one can be cleared. The compiler implements
 this trait; it cannot be implemented.

docs.body:
Returns the greatest common divisor of `a` and `b`.

 `gcd(a, 0) == gcd(0, a) == a`, so `gcd(0, 0) == 0`. Never fails.

 Uses Euclid's algorithm with `%`, so gas depends on the inputs: one loop
 iteration per remainder step, at most 368 for `u256` operands (reached
 by consecutive Fibonacci numbers) and far fewer for typical values.

docs.body:
A collection whose elements are places in a state space, as an array's
 are places: `c[k]` names the element at `k` with no call, a path that the
 access checker sees as `c` indexed by a dynamic key, and `c[k].f = v`
 writes one field. A collection implements it by saying where an element
 lives; the compiler calls `locate` once when it opens an access to the
 element.

 The collection is pinned to its space (`Pinned`): it lives at one number
 there, and its region is its own fields at that number together with
 every location `locate` returns. The trait is unsafe to implement: the
 access checker relies on `locate` returning locations within that region,
 and separated lanes for distinct keys, without checking it, so each
 implementation is an `unsafe impl` that asserts both. A memory
 collection, whose elements live in an allocation it owns, implements
 `Index` instead.

docs.body:
How a place-indexed collection encodes an element it packs into a lane:
 `BITS` bits of a storage word, `offset` bits above its low end, shared
 with the neighbouring elements. Reading the element loads the word and
 decodes it with `get`; writing it stores the word `set` returns, so only
 the element's bits change. A `BITS` above 128 packs nothing: the element
 keeps its type's storage layout, `core::intrinsic::storage_slots<T>()`
 slots, which a collection's `locate` steps by from one element to the
 next.

docs.body:
Allocates `size` bytes and returns a pointer to the first byte.
 The allocation establishes a byte extent, not initialized typed contents.
 Native `ref`/`mut` slots require a valid typed store before they are read.
 Every allocation goes through `alloc_bytes`, which bounds the size, or
 `alloc_bytes_unchecked`, whose callers bound it.

docs.body:
A range from start to end (exclusive).

 The bounds can be either compile-time known (`Known<N>`) or runtime (`Unknown`).
 This allows for zero-cost ranges when bounds are known at compile time:
 - `Range<Known<0>, Known<10>>` - 0 words (fully const)
 - `Range<Known<0>, Unknown>` - 1 word (common `0..n` pattern)
 - `Range<Unknown, Unknown>` - 2 words (fully dynamic)

items.name: array_view

docs.body:
A lazy, validated view of a Solidity ABI `T[]` value inside a `ByteInput`.

 This is the equivalent of a Solidity `T[] calldata` parameter: creating
 the view validates only the array frame (the offset word, the length
 word and the element heads), and elements are decoded one at a time on
 access. Nothing is copied to memory, so reading a few elements of a large
 or deeply nested array costs gas proportional to what is read rather than
 to the size of the whole argument. Use `DynArray<T>` instead when the
 whole array is needed in memory (for example to return or re-encode it).

 Create a view with `decode_array_view_at` (any input) or
 `CallData::array_view` (current calldata). All validation failures revert
 with empty returndata, like Solidity ABI decoding errors; an element
 index out of range reverts with Solidity `Panic(0x32)`, like indexing a
 Solidity calldata array.

docs.body:
The raw first word of element `index`'s head, at
 `heads_pos() + index * stride`.

 For dynamic `T` this is the element's tail offset relative to
 `heads_pos()`, exactly as encoded and without any validation. For
 static `T` it is the first word of the element's inline encoding,
 also unvalidated (e.g. an `Address` with dirty upper bits is returned
 as is). The word itself always lies within the input, as the
 construction checks cover all element heads. A zero-sized static `T`
 (such as `()`) has no head, so the result is 0 and nothing is read.

 Reverts with `Panic(0x32)` if `index >= len()`.

docs.body:
Like `element_pos`, but without validating the tail of a dynamic
 element: for dynamic `T` it returns `heads_pos() + head_word(index)`
 computed modulo `2**256`, like the `add` of a hand-written decoder
 (`heads + calldataload(heads + index * 32)`). For static `T` it is
 identical to `element_pos`.

 The returned position may lie beyond the end of the input or wrap
 around. Only use it when the caller validates the element's encoding
 itself, or when reads past the end are harmless for the input at
 hand, as with `CallData`, where out-of-range reads yield zeros. Prefer
 `element_pos`, `get` or the lazy element accessors otherwise.

 Reverts with `Panic(0x32)` if `index >= len()`.

Byte position in `input` where the encoding of element `index` starts.

 For static `T` this is the element's inline head. For dynamic `T` it is
 the element's tail, after checking that the tail offset is below
 `2**64` and does not overflow, and that the element's own head

 field decoders or with
 `decode_array_view_at(input, base: pos, head_pos: field_offset)`.

 Reverts with `Panic(0x32)` if `index >= len()`.

docs.body:
Decode element `index`.

 The element is decoded with the regular Solidity ABI decoder, so each
 word is validated like a function parameter: an `Address` or narrow
 integer with dirty upper bits, a `bool` other than 0 or 1, or a tail
 of a dynamic element that is out of bounds or at an offset of `2**64`
 or more reverts with empty returndata. Only element `index` is read
 and validated.

 Dynamic elements (`Bytes`, nested `DynArray`s, structs with dynamic
 fields) are copied into memory; use `bytes_at`, `string_at` or
 `array_at` to keep them lazy instead.

 Reverts with `Panic(0x32)` if `index >= len()`.

pub fn decode_array_view<T, I>(_ input: own I) -> ArrayView<I, T>
    where I: ByteInput + Copy, T: AbiSize

docs.body:
View an ABI `T[]` inside `input`.

 `base` is the start of the enclosing ABI tuple (offsets are relative to
 it) and `head_pos` is the byte offset of the array's head word within
 that tuple. For the `k`-th argument of an external call use
 `CallData::with_base(4)` with `base: 0, head_pos: k * 32` (or
 `CallData::array_view`).

 Performs the checks Solidity applies to a `T[] calldata` parameter and
 reverts with empty returndata if any fails:
 - the head word lies within the input;
 - the array's length word at `base + offset` lies within the input;
 - all `len` element heads lie within the input, that is
   `base + offset + 32 + len * stride <= input.len()`, where `stride` is
   `T::HEAD_SIZE` for static `T` and 32 for dynamic `T`.

 An input is shorter than `2**64` bytes (`ByteSource::size`), so offset and
 length words of `2**64` or more are rejected, like in Solidity. A length is
 also limited below `2**64` for a zero-sized element type, whose elements
 take no input.

 Element tails of dynamic `T` are not inspected here; they are validated
 when accessed, exactly like Solidity. Solidity also rejects calldata
 shorter than the complete static head of all parameters before running
 the function body; this function checks only the head word it reads.

docs.body:
The element at `index`. Reverts with Solidity `Panic(0x32)` if
 `index >= len()`.

 A read past the end fails loudly (like `DynString::byte_at`) instead
 of reading zero: for typed elements a silent zero is indistinguishable
 from real data.

 Elements decode through the regular Solidity ABI path, so the same
 canonicalization rules as parameter decoding apply. Decoding the
 containing `DynArray` copies the payload verbatim without inspecting
 static element words, so e.g. an `Address` element with dirty upper
 bits only reverts once it is read here — exactly as it would when
 decoded as a standalone parameter.

 Any ABI element works: one-word values, multi-word static structs
 and tuples, and dynamic elements such as `Bytes` or structs holding
 them, whose tail offset is validated against the array payload.

 `bytes[]` built by `dyn_array_from([a, b])` encodes like Solidity's

 distinct non-copyable elements in a loop. For a non-`Copy` ABI struct,
 encode individual values with `encode_abi_payload` instead.

docs.body:
Maps a Fe type to its Solidity ABI type name.

 The compiler uses this trait to build event signatures at compile time.
 For example, `u256::SOL_TYPE` is `"uint256"` and `Address::SOL_TYPE` is
 `"address"`. The `#[event]` desugaring generates a `TOPIC0` constant
 from these values:

 ```
 const TOPIC0: u256 = keccak((Transfer::SOL_TYPE, "(", Address::SOL_TYPE, ",", u256::SOL_TYPE, ")"))
 ```

 Implement this trait for custom types to use them as event fields.

 static composites whose ABI head occupies more than one word.

 punctuation, e.g. `(uint256,address)`.

docs.body:
Solidity `bytesN` for `1 <= N <= 32`.

 The ABI representation is a single word with the `N` bytes left-aligned and
 the remaining bytes zero-padded. `val` stores the human-sized value
 right-aligned; e.g. `FixedBytes<4> { val: 0x01ffc9a7 }` encodes as
 `0x01ffc9a7...00`.

 Use the aliases `Bytes1` through `Bytes32` for Solidity-compatible source
 signatures. Encoding or decoding an unsupported width (`N == 0` or
 `N > 32`) reverts.

 offset of the dynamic head within that payload.

 revert with empty returndata. An input is shorter than `2**64` bytes
 (`ByteSource::size`), so offset and length words of `2**64` or more are
 rejected, like in Solidity.

docs.body:
Allocate a `Bytes` of byte length `LEN` from `N` u256 words.

 `LEN <= N * 32`; slack in the last canonical word is preserved in memory but
 outside `LEN` is not part of the canonical value. Extra words beyond the
 canonical padded length are ignored. The function reverts with empty
 returndata when `LEN > N * 32`.

 This is useful for fixed-size byte sequences that are passed through
 Solidity ABI dynamic `bytes`, such as a 48-byte BLS public key backed by two
 words.

docs.body:
Whether available >= ceil(minimum * 64 / 63) + reserved + 40,000.
 Implements the conservative EIP-150 inequality without multiplication or
 addition overflow, including arbitrary u256 inputs. The reserve is extra
 gas beyond the 1/64 retained by EIP-150. This checks gas only, not balance,

fn is_canonical_ecrecover_signature(v: u256, r: u256, s: u256) -> bool {
    (v == 27 || v == 28)
        && r > 0
        && r < SECP256K1_ORDER
        && s > 0
        && s <= SECP256K1_HALF_ORDER
}

pub trait Ctx: EvmCapabilitySeal {
    fn address(self) -> Address

    fn block_number(self) -> u256
    fn prevrandao(self) -> u256
    fn gaslimit(self) -> u256
    fn chainid(self) -> u256
    fn basefee(self) -> u256
    fn selfbalance(self) -> Wei
    fn blockhash(self, _: u256) -> u256
    fn blobhash(self, _: u256) -> u256
    fn blobbasefee(self) -> u256

}

docs.body:
Keccak256 of the init code `create2<C>(value, args, salt)` deploys: `C`'s
 creation code as embedded in the current contract, followed by the
 ABI-encoded constructor `args` (pass `()` for a contract whose `init`
 takes no arguments).

 This is the `init_code_hash` input of `create2_address`. The creation code
 is copied to fresh memory with `CODECOPY` and hashed there, so the cost
 grows with its size (about 9 gas per 32-byte word plus memory expansion,
 on top of encoding `args`). Contracts that derive many addresses usually
 compute the hash once, e.g. in `init`, and store it.

docs.body:
Call with an explicit gas allotment and a caller reserve. An Err means
 the budget was insufficient and no external call was made. Ok contains
 EVM success/failure; it does not imply target code exists.

 Input is copied before measuring gas to pay memory expansion up front.
 No returndata is copied, so an adversarial return cannot consume the
 reserve. The outcome reports its full length. Revert data is not bubbled.

 See calls::has_min_gas for the EIP-150 admission rule and gas-schedule
 assumptions. The requested gas is forwarded exactly (plus the EVM's
 value stipend); admission is conservative and may reject feasible calls.

docs.body:
Revert with the current returndata if there is any, otherwise with the
 custom error `error`.

 This is OpenZeppelin's `Address.verifyCallResult` fallback: after a failed
 call, a callee's reason (custom error, `Error(string)`, `Panic`, raw bytes)
 is bubbled unchanged, and a callee that reverted without data (or a
 failure with no returndata, such as a call running out of gas) gets a
 descriptive error instead of an empty revert. The returndata is read
 directly from the EVM; the current returndata must be the failed call's.

Call `safeTransferFrom(owner, receiver, id, amount, data)` on `token`
 without reverting.

 Returns `NoCode` without calling if `token` has no code (checked before

 all available gas, copies no returndata, and returns `Ok` if the call
 succeeded (any returndata is ignored) or `Reverted` if it failed. Never
 returns `BadReturn`. The receiver's `onERC1155Received` hook is the
 token's responsibility.

docs.body:
Call `transferFrom(owner, receiver, amount)` on `token` without reverting.

 Forwards all available gas and copies at most 32 bytes of returndata, so
 an oversized return costs the caller no copy or memory expansion. The
 outcome is:

 - `Reverted` if the call failed; the revert payload is left in the
   returndata buffer
 - `Ok` if the call returned at least 32 bytes whose first word is exactly
   1 (not merely nonzero), ignoring any further bytes
 - `Ok` if the call returned no data and `token` has code (tokens such as
   USDT that return nothing)
 - `NoCode` if the call returned no data and `token` has no code. The code
   size is checked only on this path, after the call, so compliant tokens
   pay nothing extra.
 - `BadReturn` otherwise: `false`, any other word such as 2, or 1 to 31
   bytes of returndata

Call `transferFrom(owner, receiver, token_id)` on `token` without
 reverting.

 Returns `NoCode` without calling if `token` has no code (checked before
 the call, like a Solidity interface call and Seaport). Otherwise forwards
 all available gas, copies no returndata, and returns `Ok` if the call
 succeeded (any returndata is ignored, since ERC721 `transferFrom` returns
 nothing) or `Reverted` if it failed. Never returns `BadReturn`.

 Like ERC721 `transferFrom`, this does not call `onERC721Received`; use
 `check_on_received` for that.

docs.body:
The root implied by `leaf` at position `index` of a positional tree.

 At level `i` (0 = the leaf), bit `i` of `index` gives the side of the
 current node: `1` means it is the right child, so the parent is
 `keccak256(abi.encode(proof[i], node))`; `0` means it is the left child
 and the parent is `keccak256(abi.encode(node, proof[i]))`. For a complete
 tree of height `proof.len()` this makes `index` the leaf's position
 counted from the left. Bits at or above `proof.len()` are ignored, and
 an empty proof yields `leaf` itself.

 This is the Seaport bulk order proof walk (`_computeBulkOrderProof`,
 with the 3-byte key as `index`), before its final typehash step.

docs.body:
A storage-backed value guarded by a transient reentrancy lock.

 The lock bit lives in transient storage at the slot number its `lock`
 field takes, which no other storage or transient state shares. [`Mutex::lock`] and [`Mutex::unlock`] bracket a window
 across external calls; entry points that may be reentered take the lock
 with [`Mutex::try_lock`] and back off when it is held. The value is
 reached through short projections, which cannot be held across the
 external call the lock guards.

docs.body:
Writes the packed bytes at `dest` and returns how many were written,
 reverting with `Panic(0x01)` rather than write more than `room` bytes.

 The caller must ensure that `dest` has room for `room` bytes plus 32
 bytes of slack in a live allocation, because word-sized values are
 written with one full-word store. `room` comes from the caller's own
 `packed_width()` calls, which a safe implementation need not answer
 the same way twice, so implementations check it.
 The default goes through a `Packed` builder; std's implementations
 store their bytes directly.

docs.body:
Imperative builder for packed byte payloads.

 A bump-allocated memory buffer with byte-precise appends. Writes
 never touch memory beyond the buffer's current capacity, and the
 buffer grows (copy-on-grow, doubling) whenever an append would
 exceed it — a wrong capacity hint can cost a copy, never a panic
 or memory corruption. Growth moves the buffer, which is safe
 because the base pointer is never exposed before the terminal ops.

 Reads go straight to the buffer with `RETURNDATACOPY`, so returndata can
 be inspected or ABI-decoded in place without first copying all of it into

 through this view, like `CallData::with_base`.

 The view is not a snapshot: every external call or contract creation
 replaces the returndata buffer, and later reads see the new contents.

Whether `data` starts with the selector of the custom error `E`.

 Only the selector is compared: unlike `is_error`, the length of the rest
 is not checked, so data that starts with `E`'s selector but is too short
 or too long to be an `E` still matches, like Solidity's
 `bytes4(reason) == E.selector`. Use `is_error` to also require the length
 of an encoded `E`.

 buffer compare `revert_selector(ReturnData::new())` with `E`'s selector.

 `E`'s selector, and the ABI payload after it is exactly `E`'s encoded
 size when `E` is static, or at least `E`'s head size when `E` has
 dynamic fields (whose tails are not validated).

 payload", without decoding field values. Use `has_selector` to match
 on the selector alone.

 `data` is typically `CallOutcome::returndata()`; for the live returndata
 buffer use `revert_selector(ReturnData::new())` and `ReturnData::len`.

docs.body:
The message of a Solidity `Error(string)` revert, accepted and rejected
 exactly like Solidity's `catch Error(string memory reason)` clause.

 Returns `None` (the clause would not match) unless all of these hold:
 - `data` is at least 68 bytes and starts with `0x08c379a0`;
 - the string offset `o` (word at byte 4) is at most `2^64 - 1` and
   `o + 36 <= len`;
 - the string length `n` (word at byte `4 + o`) is at most `2^64 - 1` and
   `o + 36 + n <= len`.

 Like Solidity, the offset need not be 32, trailing bytes and missing tail
 padding are allowed, and the bytes are not checked to be valid UTF-8.
 The message is copied into a fresh `DynString`.

docs.body:
Whether `signature` is valid for `signer` over `digest`: true if it
 canonically recovers (`recover`) to `signer`, otherwise the result of
 `is_valid_erc1271_signature_now`.

 This is OpenZeppelin 4.x `SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow` (also
 Solady's order): ECDSA is tried first regardless of the signer's code, so
 an EIP-7702 delegated EOA is accepted by its key. OpenZeppelin 5.x instead
 skips ECDSA for signers with code. An ECDSA mismatch always costs one
 `STATICCALL`, which to an account without code returns false.

docs.body:
Pack a `uint64` SSZ basic value into a 32-byte chunk.

 SSZ basic integers are little-endian and right-padded with zeros
 inside the chunk. For `uint64` that means: 8 LE bytes occupy the
 **high** 8 bytes of the u256 word (offsets 0..8 of the memory
 chunk), the remaining 24 bytes are zero.

 Equivalent reference form (slower):
 ```ignore
 var chunk: u256 = 0
 for i in 0..8 { chunk |= ((value >> (i*8)) & 0xff) << (256 - (i+1)*8 ... )) }
 ```

 The implementation byte-swaps the low 64 bits with three SWAR-style
 passes (8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit), then shifts the result into the
 high 8 bytes of the chunk. The `#[arithmetic(unchecked)]` is
 required because the byte-swap relies on wrapping multiplication-
 free shifts that the bounds checker can't otherwise prove safe.

docs.body:
Merkleize a tuple of pre-computed chunk roots into a single SSZ
 hash-tree-root.

 The tuple shape encodes the number of chunks in the value. For
 `N` chunks the trait pads to the next power of two (`P >= N`)
 with zero leaves on the right and computes the root of the
 balanced binary tree over `P` leaves.

 Implemented for tuple arities 1..=16, covering all SSZ containers
 in current consensus types (the wider beacon-chain containers like
 `BeaconBlockBody` decompose into sub-roots first, then merkleize
 at arity ≤16).

 Usage:
 ```ignore
 let root: u256 = (chunk0, chunk1, chunk2, chunk3).merkleize()
 ```

docs.body:
Mix the actual element count of an SSZ list into its Merkle root.

 SSZ distinguishes `Vector[T, N]` (fixed length, root = merkleize of
 chunks) from `List[T, N]` (variable length, root = `sha256(M || L)`
 where M is the merkleized chunks padded to the type's capacity N
 and L is the length as a `uint64` chunk).

 Call this on the merkleized capacity-padded root with the actual
 element count to get the canonical `List` root. The deposit
 contract uses it on `deposit_count` to finalize `get_deposit_root`.

items.name: StorageKey

docs.body:
A storage-backed mapping from keys `K` to values `V`, laid out like a
 Solidity `mapping`.

 A map is a storage collection: it lives at its place in storage, which
 takes one slot of its container, never written, as a Solidity mapping's
 does, and it is never copied or moved. The value at `key` occupies the
 slots from `keccak256(key ++ slot)` onwards,
 laid out like any value of type `V` in storage, including packed struct
 fields, so a map in a map's value derives its slot from its entry's. The
 entries are persistent, so a map cannot lie in transient storage.
 `map[key]` names that entry's place: `map[key].f += 1` reads and writes
 one field, and `let e = mut map[key]` binds the entry. Keys use the stable
 encoding `StorageKey` defines.

docs.body:
A storage-backed packed array of fixed-bit-width integer lanes, indexed
 by any `u256`, with no length: a packed map of small integers.

 Index `i` is lane `i % (256 / BITS)` of word `i / (256 / BITS)`, and word
 `w` lies at `keccak256(slot) + w`, from the array's slot on like a Solidity
 dynamic array's data. Consecutive indices share words, so dense integer
 indices (token IDs, user IDs, order IDs, sequence positions) pack well;
 addresses or hashes would take a word each and belong in a `StorageMap`.
 Every index reads as zero until it is set.

 The words have no bound: the indices reach `BITS / 256` of all storage
 from `keccak256(slot)` on, which can include another field's slots or a
 map's entries. Keep indices in a range the contract controls rather than
 passing an untrusted `u256` through.

 `BITS` must be a power of two that divides 256 — one of
 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The constraint is enforced at compile time
 via `PackedBits<BITS>: ValidPackedBits`; invalid widths fail type-checking
 with a "trait bound is not satisfied" error.

 The array lives at its storage place, which takes one slot. A
 `StoragePackedArray` in a contract field, a struct or a map value is its
 own array.

 # Example

 ```fe
 struct Store {
     order_status: StoragePackedArray<8>,
     order_tier:   StoragePackedArray<4>,
 }

 fn write_order_status() uses (store: mut Store) {
     store.order_status.set(42, 1)
 }
 ```

docs.body:
Process CPU time in host clock ticks. Negative readings are unavailable.

 The origin is unspecified. Subtract readings to measure CPU work, excluding
 time waiting for input. Tick frequency is the host C CLOCKS_PER_SEC constant;
 it is not necessarily the same on different platforms. Supported native hosts
 (AArch64 macOS and x86_64 Linux) use a 64-bit clock_t. Its bits are read
 as i64: the C failure sentinel is -1, and counts beyond i64::MAX are negative.

 dynamic offsets are relative to.

items.name: bytes_from_word

items.name: bytes_from_words_prefix
items.summary:
Allocate a `Bytes` of byte length `LEN` from `N` u256 words.

 `LEN <= N * 32`; slack in the last canonical word is preserved in memory but
 outside `LEN` is not part of the canonical value.

A view over the current EVM calldata.

 `base` marks the first byte visible through this view.

items.summary:
Whether available >= ceil(minimum * 64 / 63) + reserved + 40,000.
 Implements the conservative EIP-150 inequality without multiplication or
 addition overflow, including arbitrary u256 inputs.

items.summary:
Revert with the current returndata if there is any, otherwise with the
 custom error `error`.

 This is OpenZeppelin's `Address.verifyCallResult` fallback: after a failed
 call, a callee's reason (custom error, `Error(string)`, `Panic`, raw bytes)
 is bubbled unchanged, and a callee that reverted without data (or a
 failure with no returndata, such as a call running out of gas) gets a
 descriptive error instead of an empty revert.

The selector followed by the message's ABI payload, encoded in place in

Encode a custom error (4-byte selector + ABI-encoded fields) into freshly

ABI-encode a message (4-byte selector + payload) into freshly allocated
 memory without performing a call.

Keccak256 of the init code `create2<C>(value, args, salt)` deploys: `C`'s

Address at which `create2<C>(value, args, salt)` executed by `deployer`
 creates the contract: `create2_address(deployer, salt, init_code_hash<C>(args))`.

 The deployment itself may still fail (e.g.

items.name: read_storage_word
items.summary:
Copies one word from the current contract's persistent storage.

 Any slot is permitted, including declared contract state.

items.name: read_transient_word
items.summary:
Copies one word from the current contract's transaction-local storage.

 This has the same authority and interference rules as `read_storage_word`.
 Every word is a valid `u256`.

items.name: revert
items.summary: Revert the current transaction with ABI-encoded data.

items.name: revert_bytes
items.summary: Revert with `data` as the raw revert payload.

items.summary: Revert with a Solidity-compatible custom error.

items.summary: Perform a raw `STATICCALL` and ABI-decode the returndata on success.

items.name: storage_at
items.summary:
The `T` at storage slot `slot`, as a storage place to read, or to write
 where its use asks for `mut`.

items.name: Address
items.summary:
EVM address (20 bytes).

 Represented as a single `u256` ABI word with the address in the low 160
 bits and every higher bit zero, as the EVM and Solidity see an address.

items.name: CallOutcome
items.summary: Owned returndata from a typed, non-bubbling EVM call.

items.name: Evm
items.summary: Default EVM effect provider (zero-sized).

items.name: RawCallOutcome
items.summary: Metadata returned by a low-level EVM call.

items.name: TSlot
items.summary:
A transient storage cell holding a `T`, kept in a storage struct.

 A `TSlot` is pinned to transient storage: its value lies there from the
 cell's number on, taking as many numbers as it has words, and the layout
 keeps them apart from other transient state.

items.name: Call
items.summary: High-level contract calls with ABI encoding/decoding.

items.name: Contract
items.summary: Metadata for deployable high-level contracts.

items.name: Ctx
items.summary: EVM execution context (env access).

items.name: RawOps
items.summary: Access to low-level EVM op functions (excluding raw stack ops).

items.name: RawStorage
items.summary:
Low-level raw storage operations.

 A raw slot must not belong to anything the compiler allocated, such as a
 contract field: the access checker does not see accesses through it.

items.name: Super
items.summary: Combined EVM capability: provides all EVM effects.

items.name: DOMAIN_TYPEHASH
items.summary: `keccak256("EIP712Domain(string name,string version,uint256 chainId,address verifyingContract)")`.

items.name: digest
items.summary:
EIP-712 typed-data digest,
 `keccak256(0x19 ++ 0x01 ++ domain_separator ++ struct_hash)`, like
 OpenZeppelin's `MessageHashUtils.toTypedDataHash`.

items.name: domain_separator
items.summary: `keccak256(abi.encode(DOMAIN_TYPEHASH, name_hash, version_hash, chain_id, verifying_contract))`.

items.name: Domain
items.summary:
An EIP-712 domain with the separator cached for the chain and contract
 that created it.

items.name: try_safe_batch_transfer_from
items.summary:
Call `safeBatchTransferFrom(owner, receiver, ids, amounts, data)` on
 `token` without reverting, with the same classification as
 `try_safe_transfer_from`.

items.name: try_safe_transfer_from
items.summary:
Call `safeTransferFrom(owner, receiver, id, amount, data)` on `token`
 without reverting.

 Returns `NoCode` without calling if `token` has no code (checked before
 the call, like a Solidity interface call and Seaport).

items.name: supports_erc165
items.summary: Whether `account` implements ERC-165 itself.

items.name: supports_interface
items.summary: Whether `account` implements ERC-165 and `interface_id`.

items.name: supports_interface_unchecked
items.summary:
`supportsInterface(interface_id)` without checking ERC-165 support first:
 true for a successful call returning at least one nonzero word.

items.name: empty_return_without_code
items.summary:
True if the token call just performed succeeded with empty returndata and
 `token` has no code, i.e.

items.name: safe_approve
items.summary:
Call `approve(spender, amount)` on `token`, reverting unless the approval
 succeeded under SafeERC20 rules.

items.name: safe_transfer
items.summary:
Call `transfer(receiver, amount)` on `token`, reverting unless the
 transfer succeeded under SafeERC20 rules.

items.name: safe_transfer_from
items.summary:
Call `transferFrom(owner, receiver, amount)` on `token`, reverting unless
 the transfer succeeded under SafeERC20 rules.

Call `approve(spender, amount)` on `token` without reverting; see
 `try_transfer_from` for the classification.

items.name: try_transfer
items.summary:
Call `transfer(receiver, amount)` on `token` without reverting; see
 `try_transfer_from` for the classification.

items.name: try_transfer_from
items.summary:
Call `transferFrom(owner, receiver, amount)` on `token` without reverting.

 Forwards all available gas and copies at most 32 bytes of returndata, so
 an oversized return costs the caller no copy or memory expansion.

items.name: ENTRY_POINT_V07
items.summary: The canonical EntryPoint v0.7 deployment.

items.name: ENTRY_POINT_V08
items.summary: The canonical EntryPoint v0.8 deployment.

items.name: PACKED_USEROP_TYPEHASH
items.summary: `keccak256` of the EIP-712 type of a user operation in EntryPoint v0.8.

items.name: SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED
items.summary: Validation data of a user operation whose signature is invalid.

items.name: SIG_VALIDATION_SUCCESS
items.summary:
Validation data of a user operation whose signature is valid, with no
 time range.

items.name: PostOpMode
items.summary: Why the EntryPoint calls `postOp`, the Solidity `IPaymaster.PostOpMode`.

items.name: pack_validation_data
items.summary:
`SIG_VALIDATION_SUCCESS` or `SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED` packed with a time
 range, like OpenZeppelin's `ERC4337Utils.packValidationData(bool, ...)`.

items.name: pay_prefund
items.summary:
Send `missing_account_funds` to the caller (the EntryPoint), with all
 remaining gas.

items.name: require_entry_point
items.summary: Revert with `AccountUnauthorized` unless the caller is `entry_point`.

items.name: require_paymaster_entry_point
items.summary: Revert with `PaymasterUnauthorized` unless the caller is `entry_point`.

items.name: validate_user_op
items.summary:
`validateUserOp` of an account whose signatures `signer` checks, like
 OpenZeppelin's `Account.validateUserOp`: reverts with
 `AccountUnauthorized` unless called by `entry_point`, checks
 `user_op.signature` over `user_op_hash`, pays the prefund and returns
 `SIG_VALIDATION_SUCCESS` or `SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED`.

items.name: AccountMsg
items.summary: Messages the EntryPoint sends to accounts.

items.name: PaymasterMsg
items.summary: Messages the EntryPoint sends to paymasters.

items.name: AccountUnauthorized
items.summary:
The validator of an account was called by an address other than the
 EntryPoint.

items.name: PackedUserOperation
items.summary:
A user operation as the v0.7 and v0.8 EntryPoint pass it to accounts and
 paymasters, the Solidity `PackedUserOperation`.

 `account_gas_limits` packs the verification gas limit (high 128 bits) and
 the call gas limit (low 128 bits); `gas_fees` packs the max priority fee
 (high 128 bits) and the max fee per gas (low 128 bits).

items.name: PaymasterUnauthorized
items.summary:
The validator of a paymaster was called by an address other than the
 EntryPoint.

items.name: ValidationData
items.summary:
Unpacked validation data: an `aggregator` (zero for a valid signature,
 `Address { inner: 1 }` for `SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED`, otherwise a signature
 aggregator) and the time range `valid_after..=valid_until` in which the
 operation is valid.

items.name: UserOpSigner
items.summary:
The account's own signature check for `validate_user_op`, OpenZeppelin's
 `_rawSignatureValidation`.

items.name: ON_ERC721_RECEIVED
items.summary: `IERC721Receiver.onERC721Received.selector`.

items.name: check_on_received
items.summary:
Call `onERC721Received(operator, from, token_id, data)` on `receiver`
 without reverting, as done after an ERC721 safe transfer
 (OpenZeppelin `ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received`).

 Returns `NoCode` without calling if `receiver` has no code; ERC721 treats
 such receivers as accepting.

items.name: try_transfer_from
items.summary:
Call `transferFrom(owner, receiver, token_id)` on `token` without
 reverting.

 Returns `NoCode` without calling if `token` has no code (checked before
 the call, like a Solidity interface call and Seaport).

items.name: Event
items.summary: Trait implemented by `#[event]` structs.

items.name: TopicValue
items.summary:
Converts an indexed event field value to a `u256` log topic.

 The `#[event]` desugaring generates `value.as_topic()` calls for each
 `#[indexed]` field.

items.name: Enqueued
items.summary: The outcome of [`StorageHeap::enqueue`].

items.name: HeapIsEmpty
items.summary: `pop` or `replace` on an empty heap.

items.name: Reverse
items.summary: Reverses the order of `T`, so a `StorageHeap<Reverse<T>>` is a max-heap.

items.name: StorageHeap
items.summary:
A min-heap of `T` in storage: `root` and `pop` return the smallest
 element.

items.name: code_region_offset
items.summary: Return the code offset/size for the call graph rooted at `func`.

items.name: contract_field_slot
items.summary:
Returns the fixed storage slot offset (in 32-byte slots) for the given contract field
 index within the current contract.

items.name: array_data_slot
items.summary:
The first slot of the elements of a Solidity dynamic array at slot
 `root`, and of the data of a long `bytes` or `string` there:
 `keccak256(abi.encode(root))`.

items.name: element_location
items.summary:
The location of element `index` of elements laid out from slot `first`
 like a Solidity array's: lanes of `bits` bits, `256 / bits` to a slot,
 when `bits` is at most 128 (a `LaneCodec`'s `BITS`), and otherwise
 `storage_slots<T>()` slots each, as its storage layout places it.

items.name: mapping_slot
items.summary:
The slot of `mapping[key]` for a Solidity `mapping` at slot `root`:
 `keccak256(abi.encode(key, root))`, with `key` encoded as its
 `StorageKey` implementation defines.

items.name: hash_pair_sorted
items.summary:
`keccak256(abi.encode(min(a, b), max(a, b)))`: OpenZeppelin's
 `Hashes.commutativeKeccak256` (`MerkleProof._hashPair`).

items.name: process_indexed_proof
items.summary:
The root implied by `leaf` at position `index` of a positional tree.

 At level `i` (0 = the leaf), bit `i` of `index` gives the side of the
 current node: `1` means it is the right child, so the parent is
 `keccak256(abi.encode(proof[i], node))`; `0` means it is the left child
 and the parent is `keccak256(abi.encode(node, proof[i]))`.

items.name: process_proof
items.summary:
The root implied by `leaf` and a sorted-pair `proof`:
 `node = hash_pair_sorted(node, proof[i])` for each node in order,
 starting from `leaf`.

items.name: verify
items.summary:
Whether `leaf` is proven part of the sorted-pair tree with `root`:
 `process_proof(proof, leaf) == root`.

 Same as OpenZeppelin `MerkleProof.verify`.

items.name: verify_indexed
items.summary:
Whether `leaf` sits at position `index` of the positional tree with
 `root`: `process_indexed_proof(proof, leaf, index) == root`.

items.name: ProofNodes
items.summary:
A sequence of 32-byte Merkle proof nodes, ordered from the leaf's
 sibling up to the child of the root.

items.name: multicall
items.summary:
`DELEGATECALL` every entry of `data` to `ctx.address()` in order, with
 all remaining gas, and return their returndata in the same order.

items.name: FailedCall
items.summary: A batched call failed without revert data.

items.name: Mutex
items.summary:
A storage-backed value guarded by a transient reentrancy lock.

 The lock bit lives in transient storage at the slot number its `lock`
 field takes, which no other storage or transient state shares.

items.name: sload
items.summary: Copies an arbitrary word, including declared state.

items.name: staticcall_precompile
items.summary: `STATICCALL` to a precompile.

items.name: DEFAULT_CAPACITY
items.summary: Default initial capacity (in bytes) for `Packed::new`.

items.name: check_room
items.summary: Reverts with `Panic(0x01)` when `width` bytes do not fit in `room`.

items.name: encode_packed
items.summary: Pack a value (typically a tuple) into an exactly-sized fresh buffer.

items.name: keccak_packed
items.summary: keccak256 of the packed encoding — the dominant consumer.

items.name: write_word_prefix
items.summary:
Writes the low `width` bytes of `value` big-endian at `dest` with a single
 word store (clobbering the following `32 - width` bytes) and returns `width`,
 reverting when `width` exceeds `room`.

items.name: Packed
items.summary:
Imperative builder for packed byte payloads.

 A bump-allocated memory buffer with byte-precise appends.

items.name: EncodePacked
items.summary:
A value with a tightly packed byte encoding (Solidity
 `abi.encodePacked` semantics).

items.name: choose
items.summary: A uniformly chosen element of `items`, which must not be empty.

items.name: shuffle
items.summary: Shuffles `items` in place with an unbiased Fisher-Yates shuffle.

items.name: shuffle_slice
items.summary:
Shuffles the memory viewed by `items` in place with an unbiased
 Fisher-Yates shuffle.

items.name: KeccakRng
items.summary: Solady's PRNG: each word is the keccak256 of the previous one.

items.name: ReplayRng
items.summary: Returns the given words in order and then starts over.

items.name: Rng
items.summary: A source of pseudorandom 256-bit words.

items.name: ERROR_STRING_SELECTOR
items.summary: Selector of Solidity's builtin `Error(string)`.

items.name: PANIC_SELECTOR
items.summary: Selector of Solidity's builtin `Panic(uint256)`.

items.name: decode_error_string
items.summary:
The message of a Solidity `Error(string)` revert, accepted and rejected
 exactly like Solidity's `catch Error(string memory reason)` clause.

items.name: decode_panic
items.summary:
The code of a Solidity `Panic(uint256)` revert, accepted like Solidity's
 `catch Panic(uint code)` clause: `data` is at least 36 bytes and starts
 with `0x4e487b71`; the code is the word at byte 4 and trailing bytes are
 ignored.

items.name: has_selector
items.summary:
Whether `data` starts with the selector of the custom error `E`.

 Only the selector is compared: unlike `is_error`, the length of the rest
 is not checked, so data that starts with `E`'s selector but is too short
 or too long to be an `E` still matches, like Solidity's
 `bytes4(reason) == E.selector`.

items.name: is_error
items.summary:
Whether `data` has the shape of the custom error `E`: it starts with
 `E`'s selector, and the ABI payload after it is exactly `E`'s encoded
 size when `E` is static, or at least `E`'s head size when `E` has
 dynamic fields (whose tails are not validated).

 For a static `E` this is exactly "`data` is some `revert_error(E {..})`
 payload", without decoding field values.

items.name: revert_selector
items.summary:
The 4-byte selector at the start of revert data, or `None` if `data` is
 shorter than 4 bytes.

items.name: ReturnData
items.summary:
A read-only view over the current EVM returndata buffer.

 Reads go straight to the buffer with `RETURNDATACOPY`, so returndata can
 be inspected or ABI-decoded in place without first copying all of it into
 memory (compare `copy_returndata`).

items.name: decode
items.summary: Decodes `input` as exactly one item.

items.name: encode_address
items.summary: Encodes an address as a 20-byte string.

items.name: encode_bool
items.summary: Encodes `true` as the integer 1 (`0x01`) and `false` as 0 (`0x80`).

items.name: encode_bytes
items.summary: Encodes a byte string.

items.name: encode_list
items.summary: Encodes a list of already encoded items.

items.name: encode_uint
items.summary:
Encodes an integer as its big-endian bytes without leading zeros, so
 zero is the empty string `0x80`.

items.name: Item
items.summary:
A decoded RLP item: a byte string or a list, as the range of its payload
 in the input it was decoded from.

items.name: ERC1271_MAGIC_WORD
items.summary: `isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)` selector, left-aligned in a word.

items.name: is_valid_erc1271_signature_now
items.summary:
ERC-1271 check with OpenZeppelin `isValidERC1271SignatureNow` semantics:
 `STATICCALL`s `signer.isValidSignature(digest, signature)` with all
 remaining gas and returns true only if the call succeeds and returns at
 least 32 bytes whose first word is exactly `0x1626ba7e` followed by 28
 zero bytes and `signer` has code.

items.name: is_valid_signature_now
items.summary:
Whether `signature` is valid for `signer` over `digest`: true if it
 canonically recovers (`recover`) to `signer`, otherwise the result of
 `is_valid_erc1271_signature_now`.

 This is OpenZeppelin 4.x `SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow` (also
 Solady's order): ECDSA is tried first regardless of the signer's code, so
 an EIP-7702 delegated EOA is accepted by its key.

items.name: parse
items.summary:
Decode a 65-byte `r ++ s ++ v` signature or a 64-byte EIP-2098
 `r ++ vs` compact signature, where the top bit of `vs` selects
 `v = 27 + bit` and the low 255 bits are `s`.

items.name: recover
items.summary:
`parse` then `EcdsaSig::recover`: the canonical (low `s`) signer of
 `digest`, or `None`.

items.name: recover_raw
items.summary:
`parse` then `EcdsaSig::recover_raw`: the signer of `digest` under the
 precompile's rules (high `s` accepted), or `None`.

items.name: EcdsaSig
items.summary: A decoded ECDSA signature.

items.name: SolLanes
items.summary:
How a `SolArray` packs its elements: Solidity's encoding (`SolPacked`), in
 lanes when it is at most 128 bits.

items.name: Payload
items.summary:
The words of a slot's long `bytes` or `string` payload, from
 `keccak256(slot)` on; the slot itself holds the head.

items.name: SolWord
items.summary:
A 32-byte word of Solidity-packed fields, such as the value of a storage
 slot loaded by `SolSlot::load`.

 `get` and `set` address a field by its byte offset from the low end of the
 word, with the same encoding and bounds checks as `SolSlot::read`/`write`,
 but only compute on the value: storage changes only when the word is
 written with `SolSlot::store`.

items.name: SolPacked
items.summary: A value with a fixed-width Solidity storage representation.

items.name: hash_pair
items.summary:
Hash two adjacent SSZ chunks as `sha256(left || right)`.

 This is the fundamental Merkle-tree primitive: an internal node is
 the SHA-256 of its two children's 32-byte digests.

items.name: hash_tree_root
items.summary: User-facing entry point for `HashTreeRoot`.

items.name: mix_in_length
items.summary:
Mix the actual element count of an SSZ list into its Merkle root.

 SSZ distinguishes `Vector[T, N]` (fixed length, root = merkleize of
 chunks) from `List[T, N]` (variable length, root = `sha256(M || L)`
 where M is the merkleized chunks padded to the type's capacity N
 and L is the length as a `uint64` chunk).

 Call this on the merkleized capacity-padded root with the actual
 element count to get the canonical `List` root.

items.name: serialize_u64
items.summary:
Serialize a `uint64` as a Solidity-compatible `bytes memory` value.

 Returns 8 little-endian bytes wrapped in the ABI `bytes` layout
 (length-prefixed, padded to a whole word).

items.name: u64_chunk
items.summary:
Pack a `uint64` SSZ basic value into a 32-byte chunk.

 SSZ basic integers are little-endian and right-padded with zeros
 inside the chunk.

items.name: ByteVector
items.summary:
Type-level tag for an SSZ `ByteVector[N]` (fixed-length byte
 sequence).

 This is a zero-sized marker struct used purely as a type argument
 to `hash_tree_root<T>`.

items.name: HashTreeRoot
items.summary:
Compute the SSZ hash-tree-root of a value given its bytes in memory.

 Implementors decide how many chunks the value occupies and how to
 merkleize them.

items.name: Merkleize
items.summary:
Merkleize a tuple of pre-computed chunk roots into a single SSZ
 hash-tree-root.

 The tuple shape encodes the number of chunks in the value.

items.name: ceil_words
items.summary: Round `len` up to the number of whole EVM words required to store it.

items.name: copy_input_words_to_memory

The caller must ensure that `dest` has room for `len` rounded up to whole
 words.

items.name: emit_bytes_event_view

A storage-backed mapping from keys `K` to values `V`, laid out like a

items.name: PackedWords

The words of a packed array: word `w` of the array whose place starts at

items.name: StoragePackedArray
items.summary:
A storage-backed packed array of fixed-bit-width integer lanes, indexed

 dynamic array's data.

items.name: Fn
items.summary:
Core functional abstractions built around higher-kinded types.

 - `Functor`: type constructors that can be mapped over.
 - `Applicative`: type constructors that support `pure` and `<*>`.
 - `Monad`: type constructors that support `bind`/`flat_map`.

 These traits are designed for types of kind `* -> *`, such as `Option`
 or partially applied types like `Result<E>`.
 A callable value taking the parameters its shape `A` lists:
 `Fn(own T, U) -> R` is `Fn<(own T, U), Out = R>`, and `-> _` leaves
 `Out` open.

 Core functional abstractions built around higher-kinded types.

 This module defines:
 - `Fn<shape A>` and `FnMut<shape A>`: callable values.
 - `Functor`: type constructors that can be mapped over.
 - `Applicative`: type constructors that support `pure` and `<*>`.
 - `Monad`: type constructors that support `bind`/`flat_map`.

 These traits are designed for types of kind `* -> *`, such as `Option`
 or partially applied types like `Result<E>`.
 A callable value taking the parameters its shape `A` lists:
 `Fn(own T, U) -> R` is `Fn<(own T, U), Out = R>`, and `-> _` leaves
 `Out` open. A call `f(x)` of a callable value runs its `Fn` `call`, or
 its `FnMut` `call_mut`. Closures and function items implement both traits
 at the shape of their own parameters. `uses E` is the row of effects a
 call runs: those a closure's body uses, or a function's own.

```fe
pub trait Clearable
```

 A type whose all-zero representation is a value, so a stored value is
 cleared by zeroing its slots and lanes: scalars, raw pointers and
 aggregates of clearable types without `unsafe` fields. A type with
 `unsafe` fields is not, since they carry an invariant zero need not
 satisfy; nor is a storage collection, since its entries lie outside its
 own slots, so nothing holding one can be cleared. The compiler implements
 this trait; it cannot be implemented.
fe fe core 0.1.0 lib/marker/Clearable#.name: Clearable

docs:
```fe
pub trait Pinned
```

 A type pinned to a state space: a value of it, and every place in it,
 lies in `Space` wherever it is held, so it and any type holding it are
 state-only. `Space` is `Storage` or `Transient`, or another pinned
 type's, `P::Space`. A state space starts zeroed: a slot no one wrote
 reads as zero, so state holds only types whose all-zero representation
 is a value, those without `unsafe` fields.
 A storage collection is pinned (`StateIndex`), and so is a cell such as
 `TSlot`.

```fe
pub trait Snapshot: Copy
```

 A `Copy` type a view parameter takes by copy, a *snapshot*: a scalar or a
 handle, such as `Address` or a memory buffer's handle, whose copy is all a
 callee can observe. Primitives and raw pointers are snapshots without it.
 Every other value, `Copy` or not, is viewed in place: the call reads the
 caller's place for its duration, and a projection's result over it is the
 caller's place.

```fe
pub const fn gcd(_ a: u256, _ b: u256) -> u256
```

 Returns the greatest common divisor of `a` and `b`.

 `gcd(a, 0) == gcd(0, a) == a`, so `gcd(0, 0) == 0`. Never fails.

 Uses Euclid's algorithm with `%`, so gas depends on the inputs: one loop
 iteration per remainder step, at most 368 for `u256` operands (reached
 by consecutive Fibonacci numbers) and far fewer for typical values.

```fe
pub trait LaneCodec<T>
```

 How a place-indexed collection encodes an element it packs into a lane:
 `BITS` bits of a storage word, `offset` bits above its low end, shared
 with the neighbouring elements. Reading the element loads the word and
 decodes it with `get`; writing it stores the word `set` returns, so only
 the element's bits change. A `BITS` above 128 packs nothing: the element
 keeps its type's storage layout, `core::intrinsic::storage_slots<T>()`
 slots, which a collection's `locate` steps by from one element to the
 next.

```fe
pub unsafe trait StateIndex: Pinned
```

 A collection whose elements are places in a state space, as an array's
 are places: `c[k]` names the element at `k` with no call, a path that the
 access checker sees as `c` indexed by a dynamic key, and `c[k].f = v`
 writes one field. A collection implements it by saying where an element
 lives; the compiler calls `locate` once when it opens an access to the
 element.

 The collection is pinned to its space (`Pinned`): it lives at one number
 there, and its region is its own fields at that number together with
 every location `locate` returns. The trait is unsafe to implement: the
 access checker relies on `locate` returning locations within that region,
 and separated lanes for distinct keys, without checking it, so each
 implementation is an `unsafe impl` that asserts both. A memory
 collection, whose elements live in an allocation it owns, implements
 `Index` instead.

 Equivalent to `decode_array_view_at(input, base: 0, head_pos: 0)`; use it

fe fe std 0.1.0 lib/abi/array_view/decod.name: decode_array_view

docs:
```fe
pub fn decode_array_view_at<T, I>(_ input: own I, base: u256, head_pos: u256) -> ArrayView<I, T>
    where I: ByteInput + Copy, T: AbiSize
```

 View an ABI `T[]` inside `input`.

 `base` is the start of the enclosing ABI tuple (offsets are relative to
 it) and `head_pos` is the byte offset of the array's head word within
 that tuple. For the `k`-th argument of an external call use
 `CallData::with_base(4)` with `base: 0, head_pos: k * 32` (or
 `CallData::array_view`).

 Performs the checks Solidity applies to a `T[] calldata` parameter and
 reverts with empty returndata if any fails:
 - the head word lies within the input;
 - the array's length word at `base + offset` lies within the input;
 - all `len` element heads lie within the input, that is
   `base + offset + 32 + len * stride <= input.len()`, where `stride` is
   `T::HEAD_SIZE` for static `T` and 32 for dynamic `T`.

 An input is shorter than `2**64` bytes (`ByteSource::size`), so offset and
 length words of `2**64` or more are rejected, like in Solidity. A length is
 also limited below `2**64` for a zero-sized element type, whose elements
 take no input.

 Element tails of dynamic `T` are not inspected here; they are validated
 when accessed, exactly like Solidity. Solidity also rejects calldata
 shorter than the complete static head of all parameters before running
 the function body; this function checks only the head word it reads.

```fe
pub struct FixedBytes<const N: usize>
```

 Solidity `bytesN` for `1 <= N <= 32`.

 The ABI representation is a single word with the `N` bytes left-aligned and
 the remaining bytes zero-padded. `val` stores the human-sized value
 right-aligned; e.g. `FixedBytes<4> { val: 0x01ffc9a7 }` encodes as
 `0x01ffc9a7...00`.

 Use the aliases `Bytes1` through `Bytes32` for Solidity-compatible source
 signatures. Encoding or decoding an unsupported width (`N == 0` or
 `N > 32`) reverts.

docs:
Call with an explicit gas allotment and a caller reserve. An Err means
 the budget was insufficient and no external call was made. Ok contains
 EVM success/failure; it does not imply target code exists.

 Input is copied before measuring gas to pay memory expansion up front.
 No returndata is copied, so an adversarial return cannot consume the
 reserve. The outcome reports its full length. Revert data is not bubbled.

 See calls::has_min_gas for the EIP-150 admission rule and gas-schedule
 assumptions. The requested gas is forwarded exactly (plus the EVM's
 value stipend); admission is conservative and may reject feasible calls.

```fe
pub fn process_indexed_proof<P: ProofNodes>(proof: P, leaf: u256, index: u256) -> u256
```

 The root implied by `leaf` at position `index` of a positional tree.

 At level `i` (0 = the leaf), bit `i` of `index` gives the side of the
 current node: `1` means it is the right child, so the parent is
 `keccak256(abi.encode(proof[i], node))`; `0` means it is the left child
 and the parent is `keccak256(abi.encode(node, proof[i]))`. For a complete
 tree of height `proof.len()` this makes `index` the leaf's position
 counted from the left. Bits at or above `proof.len()` are ignored, and
 an empty proof yields `leaf` itself.

 This is the Seaport bulk order proof walk (`_computeBulkOrderProof`,
 with the 3-byte key as `index`), before its final typehash step.

 A bump-allocated memory buffer with byte-precise appends. Writes
 never touch memory beyond the buffer's current capacity, and the
 buffer grows (copy-on-grow, doubling) whenever an append would

```fe
pub fn decode_error_string<I: ByteInput>(_ data: I) -> Option<DynString>
```

 The message of a Solidity `Error(string)` revert, accepted and rejected
 exactly like Solidity's `catch Error(string memory reason)` clause.

 Returns `None` (the clause would not match) unless all of these hold:
 - `data` is at least 68 bytes and starts with `0x08c379a0`;
 - the string offset `o` (word at byte 4) is at most `2^64 - 1` and
   `o + 36 <= len`;
 - the string length `n` (word at byte `4 + o`) is at most `2^64 - 1` and
   `o + 36 + n <= len`.

 Like Solidity, the offset need not be 32, trailing bytes and missing tail
 padding are allowed, and the bytes are not checked to be valid UTF-8.
 The message is copied into a fresh `DynString`.

```fe
pub trait Merkleize
```

 Merkleize a tuple of pre-computed chunk roots into a single SSZ
 hash-tree-root.

 The tuple shape encodes the number of chunks in the value. For
 `N` chunks the trait pads to the next power of two (`P >= N`)
 with zero leaves on the right and computes the root of the
 balanced binary tree over `P` leaves.

 in current consensus types (the wider beacon-chain containers like
 `BeaconBlockBody` decompose into sub-roots first, then merkleize
 at arity ≤16).


```fe
pub fn u64_chunk(_ value: u64) -> u256
```

 Pack a `uint64` SSZ basic value into a 32-byte chunk.

 SSZ basic integers are little-endian and right-padded with zeros
 inside the chunk. For `uint64` that means: 8 LE bytes occupy the
 **high** 8 bytes of the u256 word (offsets 0..8 of the memory
 chunk), the remaining 24 bytes are zero.

 Equivalent reference form (slower):
 ```ignore
 var chunk: u256 = 0
 for i in 0..8 { chunk |= ((value >> (i*8)) & 0xff) << (256 - (i+1)*8 ... )) }
 ```

 The implementation byte-swaps the low 64 bits with three SWAR-style
 passes (8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit), then shifts the result into the
 high 8 bytes of the chunk. The `#[arithmetic(unchecked)]` is
 required because the byte-swap relies on wrapping multiplication-
 free shifts that the bounds checker can't otherwise prove safe.

```fe
pub struct StoragePackedArray<const BITS: u256>
```

 A storage-backed packed array of fixed-bit-width integer lanes, indexed
 by any `u256`, with no length: a packed map of small integers.

 Index `i` is lane `i % (256 / BITS)` of word `i / (256 / BITS)`, and word
 `w` lies at `keccak256(slot) + w`, from the array's slot on like a Solidity
 dynamic array's data. Consecutive indices share words, so dense integer
 indices (token IDs, user IDs, order IDs, sequence positions) pack well;
 addresses or hashes would take a word each and belong in a `StorageMap`.
 Every index reads as zero until it is set.

 The words have no bound: the indices reach `BITS / 256` of all storage
 from `keccak256(slot)` on, which can include another field's slots or a
 map's entries. Keep indices in a range the contract controls rather than
 passing an untrusted `u256` through.

 `BITS` must be a power of two that divides 256 — one of
 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The constraint is enforced at compile time
 via `PackedBits<BITS>: ValidPackedBits`; invalid widths fail type-checking
 with a "trait bound is not satisfied" error.

 The array lives at its storage place, which takes one slot. A
 `StoragePackedArray` in a contract field, a struct or a map value is its
 own array.

 # Example

 ```fe
 struct Store {
     order_status: StoragePackedArray<8>,
     order_tier:   StoragePackedArray<4>,
 }

 fn write_order_status() uses (store: mut Store) {
     store.order_status.set(42, 1)
 }
 ```

```fe
pub fn cpu_clock_ticks() -> i64
```

 Process CPU time in host clock ticks. Negative readings are unavailable.

 time waiting for input. Tick frequency is the host C CLOCKS_PER_SEC constant;
